_meta.goal: Money flow to each district over time + who is responsible + how the system functions/dysfunctions. Pilot district: Kolkata.
_meta.rules: PDF-cited or it's a gap. Every fact carries source + source_tier. Gaps recorded in _gaps, never guessed. Footnotes in UI point to the public record.
_meta.footnotes_render: source_tier 4 (news) and 3 (wikipedia) are shown but visibly flagged as needing upgrade to a government PDF source.

coverage.note: 594 districts across 35 states/UTs. 3 hand-authored deep exemplars (Kolkata, Birbhum, Jamshedpur); the rest are honest baseline skeletons (admin-model classified, empty roster/ledger with explicit _gaps — not fabricated).

system_notes.note: Kolkata has no conventional District Magistrate/Collector. Magisterial powers vest in the Commissioner of Police (one of the oldest such posts in British India); a limited Collector post handles stamp revenue/registration; service delivery is run by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation. A standard 'who is the DM responsible for this money' question therefore has no single answer here.

MPLADS delivery in Kolkata's metro seats is recommendation-heavy but completion-poor: Kolkata Uttar completed 3 of 36 works, Kolkata Dakshin 0 of 73 (as on 2026-01-06). A WB-wide review found dense metropolitan seats show limited tangible outcomes versus rural constituencies — money flows in on paper but converts to far less on the ground.

Fiscal dependence: ~52% of Kolkata Municipal Corporation's ₹5,525 cr receipts (BE 2025-26) is Government Grant-in-Aid from Central + State governments (₹2,897 cr), versus ₹2,628 cr raised from its own sources. More than half of the city's civic money is transferred down rather than locally generated — and the budget still runs a deficit (expenditure ₹5,639.56 cr).

ledger.money_in_basis: Budget Estimate 2025-26 'Government Grant' line; explicitly Grant-in-Aids from both Central and State Governments. (RE 2024-25: ₹2,347 cr.)
ledger.intended: Civic services: water supply, solid waste, sewerage & drainage, roads, slum development, health, lighting, education.

what_happened.notes: Government grant of ₹2,897 cr is ~52% of KMC's ₹5,525 cr total receipts — over half of Kolkata's civic money flows DOWN from Central+State govt, not raised locally. Budget is in deficit (expenditure ₹5,639.56 cr > receipts ₹5,524.84 cr). Named schemes flowing through: 15th Finance Commission Health Grants, AMRUT 2.0, NMCG (river/canal cleaning), NSAP, DAY-NULM.

what_happened.notes: Only 3 of 36 recommended works completed; ₹2.25 cr spent of ~₹10 cr entitlement. Money was recommended and partly disbursed but tangible delivery is low — a 'recommended ≠ spent ≠ completed' gap.

ledger.intended: MP recommends local works; District Authority sanctions/executes/pays vendors.

what_happened.notes: 73 works recommended, ZERO completed; ₹2.74 cr spent of ~₹10 cr. Highest recommendation count among the three Kolkata-area seats, lowest completion. Stark 'money wasn't spent right' case.

system_notes.note: MGNREGS — the rural job-guarantee scheme — was FROZEN for West Bengal (and thus Birbhum) for nearly four years. The Centre stopped fund release from 9 March 2022 under Section 27 of the MGNREGA Act, citing non-compliance/corruption. Work resumed only 1 June 2026 after Supreme Court intervention. This is the opposite dysfunction to Kolkata's: not 'money came and wasn't spent', but money WITHHELD from the top — wages went unpaid for months.

Pending MGNREGS dues to West Bengal stood at ₹3,038 cr (Centre's figure, 2025 Rajya Sabha) — the highest of any state; the state claims ₹18,000 cr across MGNREGS+PMAY-G. A standard rural district like Birbhum, MGNREGS-dependent, bore the brunt: assets unbuilt, migrants displaced.

Delivery contrast: Bolpur (the Birbhum-area Lok Sabha seat) is West Bengal's TOP MPLADS performer — MP Asit Kumar Mal recommended 189 works, completed 67, and spent ₹14.27 cr (highest of all 42 WB MPs), versus Kolkata's metro seats completing 3/36 and 0/73. Rural delivery outpaced the metros.

ledger.money_in_basis: Central fund release to West Bengal FROZEN under Section 27 from 9 Mar 2022; ₹0 new central money flowed for ~4 years. Resumed 1 Jun 2026.
ledger.intended: 100 days/yr guaranteed wage employment + durable rural assets.

what_happened.notes: ₹0 central release for ~4 years; ₹3,038 cr+ dues pending to WB (Centre's figure). Wages unpaid for months; resumed only after SC intervention (work restarted 1 Jun 2026 with 1.5 cr mandays approved statewide). The dysfunction here is fund WITHHOLDING upstream, not local mis-spend.

responsible.upstream: Union Ministry of Rural Development (release authority)

ledger.through_dept: Bolpur — released via nodal District Authority
ledger.money_in_basis: ~₹10 cr cumulative entitlement; ₹14.27 cr actually spent (highest of all 42 WB MPs — includes earlier-term carryover).
ledger.intended: MP recommends local works; District Authority sanctions/executes/pays vendors.

what_happened.notes: WB's top MPLADS implementer: 67 of 189 works completed, ₹14.27 cr spent — the highest financial execution among all 42 WB MPs. A rural counter-example to Kolkata's metro under-delivery.

system_notes.note: Jamshedpur is the only major city in India with NO democratically elected municipality. It was run as a private Tata township via the Jamshedpur Notified Area Committee (JNAC), services delivered by JUSCO (a Tata Steel subsidiary). A 1993 constitutional provision for an 'industrial township' (Art. 243Q proviso) let it avoid a municipal corporation despite the 74th Amendment. So 'who is responsible for civic money' has never had a normal municipal answer here.

In 2025 the Jharkhand govt dissolved JNAC and formed the Jamshedpur Industrial Area Committee — a NOMINATED (not elected) body of 27: 6 state govt, 11 Tata Steel, 10 local. The East Singhbhum Deputy Commissioner is vice-chairperson; the district-in-charge minister chairs. MLA Saryu Roy called it unconstitutional for sidestepping the 74th Amendment's elected-local-body mandate. Tata holds the largest single bloc on the body governing the city.

system_notes.note: Begusarai is the 'industrial & financial capital of Bihar' — and its heavy industry was BUILT BY CENTRAL PUBLIC MONEY. The Barauni Refinery (IOCL), Barauni Thermal Power (NTPC), and HURL Barauni fertiliser plant are all central PSUs / PSU joint ventures. The district's economic base is, in effect, the Union government's balance sheet made physical.

HURL Barauni revived a defunct 1976 fertiliser plant (shut 1999 as unviable) with ~₹9,512 cr central investment; urea production restarted 18 Oct 2022. A case of public money re-animating dead industrial capacity — contrast with Birbhum's fund-freeze.

plants.significance: Commissioned 1964-65 with Soviet/Romanian collaboration; Bihar's only refinery. BR-9 expansion adds petrochemicals.

system_notes.note: Munger's economy rests on three HERITAGE industries, each a national 'first/oldest': ITC's cigarette factory (1907 — Asia's first cigarette production), the gun/arms factories (est. 1762, Mir Qasim era), and the Jamalpur Railway Workshop (1862 — Asia's oldest & among its largest). 2nd-highest per-capita income in Bihar after Patna (₹42,793, FY21). Contrast with Begusarai's central-PSU heavy industry.

The arms tradition has a dark fiscal side: alongside ~37 licensed BIADA gun factories, Munger became a notorious hub of ILLEGAL country-made firearms (pistols to Kalashnikovs). A licit heritage industry shadowed by an untaxed, criminal one — a governance/revenue leakage story.

plants.employment_note: Major local employer; tobacco is the district's leading export.
plants.significance: Asia's first cigarette production (1907); ITC's oldest manufacturing unit.

plants.name: Jamalpur Locomotive Workshop
plants.capacity: Asia's oldest & among largest railway workshops; 50+ acres
plants.employment_note: Major employer of the local population.
plants.significance: Founded 8 Feb 1862 by the East India Company; produces inserts, brake blocks, BOX wagons, cranes.

plants.capacity: ~37 licensed gun factories across ~8 acres (BIADA land)
plants.employment_note: Generational craft; supplied arms to the Indian Army in WWI & 1962.
plants.significance: Arms-making since 1762 (Mir Qasim era); among India's oldest surviving arms units.

system_notes.note: Kochi Municipal Corporation is ~50% grant-dependent: of ₹453 cr total revenue (audited FY24), ₹225 cr is government grant vs ₹229 cr own-source — and it runs close to balance (expenditure ₹402 cr). Comparable to Kolkata's grant-dependence but with a far healthier own-source share (₹229 cr own vs ₹184 cr tax). A relatively well-run urban local body.

Ernakulam is Kerala's commercial capital (Kochi) — port, IT (Infopark/SmartCity), shipbuilding (Cochin Shipyard, a central PSU), and the Cochin International Airport (CIAL), the world's first fully solar-powered airport and a pioneering public-private-shareholder model. Diversified base, unlike single-industry districts.

system_notes.note: BMC (Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation) is India's richest civic body. Its 2025-26 budget of ₹74,427 cr is the largest in its history — bigger than the annual budget of several Indian STATES, and ~25× Kolkata's KMC. Over a decade BMC allocated ₹2.19 lakh cr. The 'money flowing through one district' here dwarfs most state-level flows.

Like Kolkata, Mumbai's civic governance has run WITHOUT an elected body since March 2022 — the ₹74,427 cr budget was presented to a state-appointed administrator (BMC Commissioner Bhushan Gagrani), not an elected council. Elections were finally held in Jan 2026. A democratic-deficit dysfunction in the country's richest municipality.
